The Reusable Rocket Revolution — how SpaceX went from one experimental flight to dominating global launch cadence.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro — why launches matter
0:38 2007–2012: the experimental era (Falcon 1, early Falcon 9)
2:10 2013–2016: cadence starts (Falcon 9 reuse prototypes)
3:45 2017–2019: commercial growth and small-sat demand
5:20 2020–2022: Starlink, cadence explosion (61+ launches in 2022)
7:05 2023–2026: full-scale race — incumbents plateau while new players scale
8:40 Takeaways & what this means for space policy and industry
9:30 Sources & credits

What you’ll see: a chart-race across 20 years (2007–2026) comparing annual launch counts for SpaceX, Arianespace, ULA, Rocket Lab and Blue Origin. The dataset highlights two truths: reusable rockets + constellation demand drove an explosive cadence at SpaceX, and legacy operators have largely held flat or declined as market share shifted.

Call to action: Like, subscribe and hit the bell if you want more time-series visualizations of tech revolutions. Share this video if you remember the first Falcon 9 landing.

Sources & reading (representative):
- SpaceX launch logs and Starlink press releases
- FAA/NOAA launch manifest summaries
- Arianespace mission logs and press releases
- United Launch Alliance (ULA) launch history
- Rocket Lab press releases and launch manifest
- Blue Origin flight history and New Shepard manifest
- SpaceNews, Ars Technica, NASA launch summaries, Wikipedia (annual launch lists)

Note on methodology: yearly counts are compiled from public manifest and post-flight reports; suborbital New Shepard flights are included under Blue Origin; for Arianespace counts include Ariane, Vega and Soyuz missions marketed by the company.

instagram_caption:
🚀 The launch cadence that broke the sky: From a single Falcon test to hundreds a year — this chart tells the 20-year story of how modern rocketry flipped the industry.

Once upon a launchpad: in 2007 there was one experimental Falcon attempt. Fast forward to 2022 — SpaceX posted 61 orbital flights in a single year as Starlink demand and reusable boosters collided into exponential growth. By 2023 the number jumped into double digits of dozens (we record 83 launches that year), and the dataset projects a jaw-dropping ~150–200 annual flights by 2025–2026 as Starship, Starlink replenishment and commercial rideshare push cadence even higher.

Meanwhile, the old guard told a different story. Arianespace — which handled Ariane and Vega missions for decades — hovered in the mid-single-to-low-double digits, then chipped down to just a handful of flights a year as program transitions, launch consolidation and market share loss set in. ULA kept government contracts steady but did not scale proportionally to commercial demand. Rocket Lab rose from zero to a steady stream of small-sat launches (we chart a jump from 1 in 2017 to 30+ by 2023). Blue Origin appears as an incremental suborbital player early on, ramping slowly as New Glenn and other programs mature.

The turning points are unmistakable: first, reusability (Falcon 9 boosters landing and reflown). Second, the Starlink business model that turned launches into recurring operational demand. Third, the commoditization of rideshare — smallsats now make frequent launches viable for smaller companies.

Numbers matter: 2007 → SpaceX 1; 2022 → SpaceX 61; 2023 → SpaceX 83; 2024–26 → projection 110→150→200 (reflected in manifest growth and public reporting). Arianespace and ULA move from double-digit historical footprints into far smaller slices of an expanded pie.

What surprised you? Which company do you think will be the steady #2 in 2030 — legacy heavyweight or new challenger? Drop one name and why in the comments.

facebook_caption:
A 20-year launch cadence comparison reveals a dramatic industry realignment: SpaceX's growth — driven by booster reusability and the Starlink constellation — transformed it from a one-off experimental launcher in 2007 to the dominant cadence leader by the early 2020s. By contrast, legacy suppliers such as Arianespace and United Launch Alliance have maintained government and institutional roles but did not match the new commercial frequency. Rocket Lab emerged as the small-sat workhorse, while Blue Origin grew more slowly with suborbital flights and a gradual move toward orbital capability.

This dataset (2007–2026) aggregates publicly reported manifests and post-flight reports from operator press releases, FAA and mission summaries. It illustrates not only winners and losers in raw counts but the structural shift toward reusable, high-frequency operations.

Sources: SpaceX, Rocket Lab, Arianespace, ULA, Blue Origin, FAA, SpaceNews, NASA manifest summaries.
